title_original: Kader Attia outlines plans for 7th Kochi-Muziris Biennale
excerpt_original: The seventh edition of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale will explore relationship between dreams, memory and repair

blocks.caption: Kader Attia. Photo: Sam Mertens. Courtesy the artist

blocks.text: The seventh edition of the Kochi-Muziris Biennale will explore relationship between dreams, memory and repair. Artist Kader Attia , the curator of the upcoming exhibition, will look to art as a space to explore the unpredictable nature of dreams: an antithesis to the predictability of artificial intelligence (AI). For Attia, the ‘memory traces’ from which dreams emerge are responsible for shaping both inner individual and external social structures. As algorithms and AI increasingly harvest these human memory traces, Attia posits that we are losing sovereignty over the sources of our dreams.

‘The art world is one of the last spaces where society co-individuates itself. Our subjectivity is fragmented, like the internet, an intensely fragmented landscape, yet there we are tracked by the algorithm,’ said Attia in a statement. ‘Exhibitions are important because they produce emotions, activating new traces in our minds. That is how we produce traces for the future. In the same way we are the traces of our ancestors and of the millions of anonymous subjects who preceded us.’

Set across multiple venues in Kochi, Kerala from 12 December 2027 to 31 March 2028, Attia draws on the significance of the historic harbour of Kochi. The harbour itself is a bridge to multiple destinations across the Indian Ocean, and has forged a ‘hybrid identity’ in the region through layers of exchange, invasion and colonialism. Within this setting of ‘colonial dreams’, Attia looks to reclaim individuality and selfhood.

‘I do not think we belong to ourselves. We do not belong to anyone. We are part of a system that interacts constantly with other subjects. As an artist, and even more as a curator, I care a lot about questioning political aspects with poetry: how a political work can have poetry, and the other way around,’ said Attia. ‘Dreams repair us, like art… and the Biennale, as well as Kerala, will give us the space-time to reclaim our sovereignty over our dreams.’
